newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - P&O won't give in on Florida fines.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - P&O won't give in on Florida fines.

text.p: British shipping group Peninsula and Oriental Steam Navigation Co on Thursday said it would not pay any fines over allegations by the U.S. State of Florida that it misled passengers on fees.

"There was no prospect that (P&O) would be paying fines in response to allegations against the cruise industry by the Florida Attorney General regarding government fees and port charges," P&O said in a statement.
The Attorney General has been investigating the way cruises have been advertised in Florida and how much money is paid to the authorities in the form of state fees.
On Tuesday, it filed a lawsuit against P&O's Princess Cruises' unit, seeking fines of $15,000 for each violation of a state consumer law.
This followed an agreement in February with Carnival Corp and other leading cruise ship companies to include most so-called port fees in advertised prices.

Other companies have settled with the Attorney General's office without admitting liability, their only penalty being to reimburse the state for the cost of the investigation. But P&O said it was not prepared to concede on the matter.
"Princess could also have settled, and indeed could do so today, but such is the strength of our case that we are not prepared to concede the principle," it said.

P&O's statement followed a sharp drop in its share price after a report in Lloyd's List newspaper on Thursday that the state of Florida was seeking up to $15,000 for each passenger that boarded at state ports over the last four years.

The shipping and insurance daily quoted Florida's Attorney-General Bob Butterworth as saying that Princess had been "pocketing" money collected as port charges that customers were led to believe was a government fee.
P&O's response lifted its share price from an intraday low of 588-3/4 pence but the share was still down 24-1/2 pence at 615p by 1220 GMT.
"It could be hugely damaging to P&O," said the head of equity trading at one London brokerage.
On Tuesday, Butterworth had said that the fees added as much as $150 to advertised ticket prices and while often described as government-imposed fees, only small amounts went to authorities.
"By keeping portions of these add-on fees for itself, Princess was able to advertise lower cruise prices than would otherwise be possible," Butterworth had said in a statement.
Princess on Tuesday said that the charges had no merit.
"We believe that our advertising in the state of Florida has always communicated to consumers the full prices of the cruise," it said in a statement.
